reasoning.text: Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the recent official six-print core CPI sample has values 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.2, with a median near 0.2 and an average near 0.25. A rounded first print of 0.3 is the natural persistence prior because BLS reports one decimal and the 2.9 percent year-over-year pace is still above target-consistent inflation.

Level, momentum, and one-off split: shelter is still adding steady positive pressure, while May's soft core goods and vehicle readings pull down the near-term center. The April 0.4 print prevents treating May's 0.2 as a new low-inflation regime; the best center is between those prints.

Policy-mechanism split: the energy shock is outside core directly, but the May evidence showed limited broad pass-through into core prices. Tariff, shipping, and energy-cost pass-through remain upside risks for July, while weak durable-goods prices and insurance normalization are downside risks.

Prior/update/interval: persistence prior is recent BLS first-print core CPI, using the Dec. 2025-May 2026 sample of 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2. Start from a 0.25 percent unrounded base, add +0.03 for shelter stickiness and possible energy/tariff pass-through, subtract -0.02 for May core-goods softness, giving 0.26 and rounding to a 0.3 percent first-print forecast. Size the 80 percent interval from recent first-print dispersion plus one-decimal release granularity: central recent mass is 0.2-0.4, widened by 0.1 on each side for July pass-through and component noise, yielding 0.1 to 0.5.

Counter-consideration and scenarios: downside outside the interval would require another broad core-goods decline plus softer shelter, producing 0.0 or below. Upside outside the interval would require energy or tariff pass-through into airfares, goods, and services at the same time, producing 0.6 or higher. The central case is sticky services with only partial goods offset.
